links.note: 341 says that whatever one has left (யாதனின் நீங்கியான்), from that one has no pain (நோதல் இலன்). 626, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, asks whether those who never guarded wealth saying 'we have got it' (பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்) would grieve saying 'we have lost it' (அற்றேமென்று). The renouncer's rule reappears in the book of wealth as a habit of mind for someone who still owns things.

341 ties freedom from pain to having left the thing itself (நீங்கியான்). 629 says one who does not crave the pleasure in pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not suffer the pain in pain; Parimelazhagar reads this as someone who goes on experiencing the pleasure without wanting it. The pairing shows the same result claimed for an inward letting go, without the outward leaving.

341's doubled யாதனின் யாதனின் ... அதனின் அதனின் allows release thing by thing: each thing left stops hurting. 343 demands that everything wanted be let go together (வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு). Parimelazhagar notices the difference under 341, calling giving up everything at once the chief way while granting that giving things up one by one still removes the pain each brings.

342 says that after renouncing, many things come about here (ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல), which Parimelazhagar takes as joys in this life. 369 says joy is unbroken even here (இன்பம் இடையறாது ஈண்டும்) once craving, the sorrow of sorrows, is gone. Both place the reward of letting go in this world (ஈண்டு), not only after death.

46 asks what a person who runs household life by the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்). 342 says that after renouncing there are many things to be had here, and urges renouncing if one wants them (வேண்டின் ... துறக்க). The conflict depends on reading புறத்தாறு as the ascetic path, as Pope does: on that reading 46's rhetorical 'what is gained?' gets the answer 'much' in 342.

36 tells one to do virtue without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது). 342's உண்டாகத் துறக்க is read by Parimelazhagar as 'renounce while there is time', i.e. in youth, so the joys last long; Manakkudavar instead reads it as 'if you want gain for your life'. On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on renunciation repeats, for renouncing, the earlier rule against postponing virtue.

126, in the householder's chapter on restraint, speaks of drawing in the five like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), which protects through seven births. 343 uses a harder verb for the renouncer: the field of the five must be killed or crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை), and every wanted thing dropped at once. Read together they show two degrees of the same discipline, withdrawal that can be reversed and destruction that cannot.

6 describes God as the one who quenched the five whose gates are the senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep to his path. 343 lays the same thing on the renouncer as a duty (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை). The renouncer is asked to do what the invocation names as the mark of the Lord.

343 says the field of the five senses must be crushed. In 1101 the lover lists the same five, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டுகேட்டு உண்டுயிர்த்து உற்றறியும் ஐம்புலனும்), and says all are found in this one woman. This is a lover's speech and not a teaching, but the shared catalogue shows the Book of Love celebrating exactly what the chapter on renunciation tells the ascetic to destroy.

344 says having nothing at all is natural to the vow (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்றின்மை) and that owning anything brings back confusion. 1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up what is desired' have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's owning nothing rests on others who produce food.

344 makes possessionlessness the nature of austerity. 263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). The pairing shows that the ascetic's having nothing is sustained by householders who keep possessions in order to give.

344 treats having nothing (ஒன்றின்மை) as the proper state of the vow. 1050 speaks of those who have nothing to enjoy (துப்புரவில்லார்) and yet do not fully renounce (துவரத் துறவாமை), calling them death to salt and gruel. Lacking things is therefore not the same as renouncing: poverty without the inner giving up is counted as a burden, not as austerity.

340 calls the life a lodger in the body (உடம்பினுள் துச்சில் இருந்த உயிர்) and asks whether it has found no home of its own. 345 draws the consequence for those set on cutting off births: even the body is surplus (உடம்பும் மிகை), so further ties make no sense. The chapter on impermanence states the body's temporary status; this verse turns it into a reason to drop attachment.

73 says the bond of the precious life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is the way that came to be joined with love, so embodiment is given a purpose. 345 says that for those undertaking to cut off births (பிறப்பறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்கு) the body itself is excess and other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) pointless. The value 73 gives the body-bond holds within the life of love; 345 marks where, for the renouncer, it stops holding.

345 says even the body is too much for one seeking to end birth. 627, in the book of wealth, says the great do not take trouble as trouble, knowing the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு). Both start from the body as a liability, but 627 uses that view to keep steady in worldly trouble while 345 uses it to argue for giving up every tie.

346 says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others even to their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). The householder's love already loosens 'mine', and even the body as 'I', by giving it to others; renunciation does it by cutting the notion itself.

50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). 346 promises the one who ends 'I' and 'mine' a world higher than the gods' (வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த உலகம்). Set side by side the two verses give a scale: the good householder reaches the gods, the renouncer goes beyond them.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றினைப் பற்றி விடாஅதவர்க்கு). 940 says that as a gambler loves the game more with each loss, the life grows more fond with each suffering it undergoes (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the object of that fondness to be the body. 940 supplies what 347 leaves unexplained: suffering does not loosen the grip but tightens it.

347 uses பற்று for attachment in general and says its holders are held by griefs. 438, on a ruler's faults, names miserliness as 'the clinging heart' (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) and says it is not to be counted with any other fault. The same word and the same refusal to let go appear in the domain of wealth, where Parimelazhagar glosses it as not releasing goods when they ought to be released.

348 says those who have thoroughly renounced have reached the goal and the rest, confused, are caught in the net (மயங்கி வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றையவர்). 266 says those who do austerity do their own work and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (மற்றல்லார் அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Both divide people in two with the same 'caught' (பட்டு/பட்டார்), and 266 names the net as desire.

348 gives the prize only to those who renounce thoroughly (தீரத் துறந்தார்). 365 says those called 'freed' are those freed of craving, and the others are not freed in that way (மற்றையார் அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்), whatever else they have given up. 365 specifies what 348's 'thoroughly' requires: the giving up must reach craving, not only things.

348 sets those who have fully renounced above everyone else. 276 says none are harder-hearted than those who have not renounced in the heart (நெஞ்சின் துறவார்) and live by deceiving as though they had (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து). The praise in 348 therefore applies to renunciation of the heart; the outward form without it is placed among the worst.

361 says craving is the seed that yields unceasing birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). 349 says the moment attachment is cut off, that cuts off birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). One verse names the cause and the other states what follows when the cause is removed; Parimelazhagar makes the same cause-and-effect point under 349.

331 calls it the lowest understanding to take what does not last for lasting (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்). 349 says that where attachment is not cut, impermanence is what is seen (மற்று நிலையாமை காணப்படும்), which Parimelazhagar reads as the round of being born and dying. The impermanence that chapter 34 asks the reader to recognise becomes, in 349, what the attached person goes on undergoing.

4 says those who reach the feet of the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) have no suffering anywhere. 350 tells one to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging (பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை), in order to let clinging go. The invocation's promise becomes a method here, and Parimelazhagar notes that பற்றற்றான் is used in keeping with the invocation chapter.

350 uses attachment to end attachment: cling to that clinging so that clinging is let go (பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு). 362 uses desire the same way: if you must want, want not being born, and that comes by wanting not-wanting (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). Both verses accept that the thing to be removed has to be turned on itself as the means.

350 says to hold to the hold of the one who has none. 359 says that if one knows the support and lives so that supports perish (சார்புணர்ந்து சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains due to come will not come. The two are built alike on a repeated word, பற்று and சார்பு, and Parimelazhagar reads the சார்பு that is known as the true reality on which all rests, so 359 states the result of the practice 350 prescribes.

351 says an inglorious birth comes from the delusion that takes what is not real for real (மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). 1002 ends with the same words: the delusion of thinking everything comes by wealth, and so hoarding without giving, produces an inglorious birth. The book of wealth applies the metaphysical formula to one concrete error, treating money as the thing that matters.

351 speaks of perceiving as real what is not real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும்). 331 has the same construction for time: perceiving as lasting what does not last (நில்லாதவற்றை நிலையின என்றுணரும்), which it calls the lowest of understandings. The two verses name the same mistake of perception, once about duration and once about reality, and 351 adds its cost: rebirth.

352 says that for those of stainless sight who have left delusion (மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு) darkness goes and joy comes. 199 uses nearly the same phrase (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்) for people who do not say meaningless things even by a slip. The person who in 352 attains release is recognised in ordinary life, in 199, by how they speak.

5 says the two kinds of deed joined with darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினை) do not attach to those devoted to the Lord's praise; Parimelazhagar glosses the darkness as delusion. 352 says darkness leaves (இருள்நீங்கி) those whose sight is free of delusion; Manakkudavar takes this darkness as ignorance, while Parimelazhagar takes it as hell and so as birth. The same darkness is removed in 5 by devotion and in 352 by clear seeing.

352 has darkness leave and joy arise for those who see truly. 243 says those whose hearts are joined with compassion do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). 243's wording supports Parimelazhagar's reading of இருள் in 352 as a dark world of suffering, and shows the book promising escape from it by compassion as well as by knowledge.

353 says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. 702 says one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை) should be held equal to a god. In both, knowing free of doubt lifts a person toward the divine, once in the knowledge of reality and once in a courtier's reading of minds.

50 says one who lives on earth (வையத்துள்) as one should is placed among the gods who dwell in the sky. 353 uses the same pair, earth and sky (வையத்தின் வானம்), and says the sky is the nearer of the two for one who is clear of doubt. The householder gets there by right living and the knower by certainty, and in both the sky is brought within reach of someone still on earth.

27 says the world lies within one who discerns the kinds of the five: taste, light, touch, sound and smell (ஐந்தின் வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு). 354 says that even when the fivefold awareness is attained (ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும்) there is no benefit for those without perception of the real. Mastery of the five, praised in 27, is declared insufficient by itself in 354.

126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection for seven. 354 says the attained fivefold awareness yields no fruit without true perception; Parimelazhagar reads ஐயுணர்வு as the mind withdrawn from the senses and held under control, and the missing fruit as release, while Manakkudavar reads it as knowing all that the five senses can know. On Parimelazhagar's reading sense-restraint earns protection across births, as 126 says, but not the end of birth.

2 asks what learning has achieved (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்) if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge. 354 says command of the five senses has no benefit (பயமின்றே) for those without perception of the real. Both verses grant an attainment and then deny its fruit when the final step is missing, learning without worship in one and discipline without insight in the other.

355 and 423 differ in a single phrase. 423: whatever is heard from whoever's mouth (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்), seeing the true thing in it is understanding; 355: whatever a thing is and of whatever nature (எத்தன்மைத் தாயினும்), seeing the true thing in it is understanding. Parimelazhagar reads மெய்ப்பொருள் in 423 as the real worth of what is said and in 355 as the reality left when the world's imposed notions are removed, so one formula serves practical judgment and knowledge of reality.

355 defines understanding as seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது) in anything. 249 uses that act as a comparison: virtue done by one without compassion is like an unclear person seeing the true thing (தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்று). 249 assumes what 355 states, that seeing the real needs a clear mind, and treats the claim of someone muddled to have seen it as empty.

355 makes seeing the true thing the definition of understanding. 857 says those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார்); Parimelazhagar takes it there as the substance of the texts on right policy that bring success. The same phrase marks, in the book of wealth, what a mind bent on quarrel cannot perceive.

398 says the learning acquired in one birth protects through seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). Learning in the book of wealth is an asset carried across births; learning that ends in seeing the real is said to end the births themselves.

356 joins learning to seeing: those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of no return. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own native understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மை யறிவே மிகும்). Study by itself does not guarantee the seeing, which is why 356 names both steps.

2 asks what use learning is to those who do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge. 356 gives learning its use: those who learn here and see the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) gain the path of no return. Both measure learning by whether it reaches what is ultimate, named as the Lord in 2 and as the true thing in 356.

356 speaks of those who learn and see the true thing; 357 adds the mind's own work: if the mind examines and knows with certainty what is (ஓர்த்து ... உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையா), one need not think of birth again. Parimelazhagar reads the two as successive means, hearing instruction in 356 and reasoned examination in 357. The printed text here has உணரான், but Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's glosses read உணரின், which the sense requires.

358 defines understanding as seeing the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு), which Parimelazhagar explains as the changeless first reality. 91 says sweet words come from the mouths of those who have seen the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்), where Parimelazhagar takes the word as virtue. The same phrase names the seer of final truth in one place and the source of kind, honest speech in the other.

351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes the unreal for real. 358 goes a step further and calls birth itself a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை); Parimelazhagar explains this as naming the effect in place of its cause. The chapter moves from delusion as the cause of birth to birth and delusion spoken of as one thing, removed together by seeing the real.

358 speaks of 'the folly called birth' departing when the real is seen. 835, in the chapter on folly in the book of wealth, says a fool can in one birth's doing make the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both tie பேதைமை to the chain of births, 358 as its root and 835 through the fool's deeds.

5 says the two kinds of deed do not attach (சேரா) to those devoted to the Lord's praise. 359 says the pains due to attach will not attach (சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்) to one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish; Parimelazhagar takes these as the fruits of stored deeds still awaiting experience, and Manakkudavar takes சார்பு itself as the hold of deeds. Devotion in 5 and knowledge with practice in 359 are credited with the same effect on karma.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold on to attachment. 359 gives the other case: for one who knows the support and lives so that supports fall away (சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains that were due do not come to cling. 347 states the bondage and 359 the way out, in the same language of things that cling.

360 says pain perishes when desire, anger and confusion perish down to their names (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் ... நாமம் கெட); Parimelazhagar glosses the three as wanting, aversion and ignorance. 4 describes God as the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet have no suffering. The state 360 sets as the goal is the nature 4 gives to the Lord, with the same result, the end of suffering.

35 defines virtue as conduct that avoids four things: envy, craving, anger and harsh speech (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). 360 names three, desire, anger and confusion, and asks that even their names be gone. Craving and anger are on both lists; the early verse asks that conduct not slip into them, the later one that they be destroyed at the root, with confusion added as the one that knowledge removes.

360 lists desire, anger and confusion as what must perish for pain to end. 431 lists three faults whose absence gives a ruler's prosperity its dignity: arrogance, anger and smallness (செருக்கும் சினமும் சிறுமையும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as pride, anger and lust. A similar triad, sharing anger and, on that gloss, desire, is the obstacle to release in one book and to good rule in the other.
